implementation_notes: Camel provides the pattern as a first-class EIP: the expression is invoked iteratively and returns the next endpoint URI, or null to end - the Routing Slip with the slip evaluated on the fly - so route definitions never enumerate the destinations and the rule source (database, registry, config service) can change without a redeploy. Keep per-exchange state in Exchange properties rather than bean fields, because the bean instance is shared across exchanges; the annotation form (@DynamicRouter) works the same way through bean integration. Prefer it when destinations are Camel endpoints and routing policy is maintained outside the route definition.
pitfalls: Returning a non-null URI forever makes the dynamicRouter loop endlessly: the terminal null is mandatory on every path, including error paths.
The bean is shared across exchanges, so an invocation counter in a field is a race - keep state on the Exchange or in Exchange properties (headers are not guaranteed to survive routing).

ignoreInvalidEndpoints defaults to false, so one stale URI in the rule base aborts the exchange; decide explicitly whether to ignore or fail, and constrain what rules may point at with allowedSchemes.

variants.name: Spring Integration mapping router with control-bus updates
variants.implementation_notes: Spring Integration treats every AbstractMappingMessageRouter (payload-type, header-value, recipient-list, expression-based) as a dynamic router because the channel-identifier-to-channel-name mapping can be changed at runtime through setChannelMapping/removeChannelMapping or replaced wholesale and atomically with replaceChannelMappings, and the documented driver for those operations is the control bus, or JMX. The static step that computes the identifier and the mutable step that resolves it to a channel are separate layers, which is what lets the same expression route to a different channel after an operational change. Use it when the message flow is a Spring Integration pipeline and routing policy should be adjustable without restarting the application context.
pitfalls: Two setChannelMapping calls leave the table in an indeterminate state between them; use replaceChannelMappings for an atomic swap.

channelKeyFallback=true lets a message address a channel by name unless a mapping overrides it - an untrusted producer can then route to an unexpected channel, including the router's own input channel.
Mutating the mapping programmatically bypasses the control bus and JMX audit trail, so route changes stop being observable.
